connection: Every later session assumes you already understand how PinkMachine19.TimeClock.sln, src/, and tests/ came to exist. This session scaffolds that layout yourself with the dotnet CLI, then goes one step further: a real solution is not just projects, it is folders inside those projects, each with one job. You build both.
objectives: Explain what a solution (.sln) is and what a project (.csproj) is, and how the two relate.
Distinguish a console application, a class library, and an xUnit test project by what each one produces.
Use dotnet new to generate a solution, a class library, a console app, and an xUnit test project.
Explain why source projects live under src/ and test projects live under tests/.
Use dotnet sln add and dotnet build to assemble and build a solution from independently created projects.
Create a standard set of purpose-named folders inside a project and explain why each one exists.
Explain why an empty folder disappears from a fresh git clone, and how a README.md prevents that.

visuals.title: A solution is a list of projects, not a project itself
visuals.explanation: PinkMachine19.TimeClock.sln does not contain code. It is a manifest that names which .csproj files belong together so one command can build or test all of them.

visuals.title: dotnet new turns a template name into a folder
visuals.explanation: dotnet new classlib -o src/PinkMachine19.TimeClock.Domain creates a folder containing PinkMachine19.TimeClock.Domain.csproj and a starter .cs file. The -o path is also where the project will live.

visuals.title: A test project is a project, with one extra job
visuals.explanation: PinkMachine19.TimeClock.Domain.Tests is an ordinary class library plus the xUnit package. Nothing about its .csproj is structurally special — only its purpose is.

visuals.title: A folder with nothing tracked inside it does not survive a clone
visuals.explanation: Git records files, not directories. An empty Validators/ folder exists on your disk but vanishes the moment someone clones the repository, unless a file — even just a README.md — lives inside it.

options: Compiled C# code for the whole application
A list of project paths and build configurations, no source code
preQuiz.explanation: A .sln file is a manifest. The code lives entirely inside the .csproj-owning folders it lists.

preQuiz.prompt: What is the structural difference between a console application project and a class library project, right after dotnet new creates each one?
options: A console app's .csproj sets OutputType to Exe and has an entry point; a class library has neither
Class libraries cannot contain any methods
xUnit test projects are console applications internally
preQuiz.explanation: A console app is built to run directly (an .exe with a Main entry point); a class library is built to be referenced by something else and has no entry point of its own.

preQuiz.prompt: You run dotnet new classlib -o src/PinkMachine19.TimeClock.Domain but never run dotnet sln add. What happens when you later run dotnet build PinkMachine19.TimeClock.sln?
options: The new project builds along with the others automatically because it's in a src/ folder
The new project is silently skipped — the solution only builds what it's told to include
dotnet build fails immediately because the folder isn't registered
preQuiz.explanation: Folder presence is not membership. A project only participates in solution-wide build/test/restore once it's listed inside the .sln file.

concept.title: A solution groups projects; a project is the buildable unit
paragraphs: A .csproj file is the actual unit the .NET toolchain compiles: it lists a target framework, its dependencies, and the source files that belong to it. Every meaningful thing — building, running, testing, publishing — ultimately happens at the level of one .csproj.

A .sln file exists one level above that. It doesn't compile to anything; it's a manifest that names a set of .csproj paths so a single command (dotnet build PinkMachine19.TimeClock.sln, dotnet test PinkMachine19.TimeClock.sln) can act on all of them together. PinkMachine19.TimeClock.sln currently lists five projects: PinkMachine19.TimeClock.Domain, PinkMachine19.TimeClock.App, PinkMachine19.TimeClock.Infrastructure, PinkMachine19.TimeClock.Web, and PinkMachine19.TimeClock.Domain.Tests — you can see this yourself with dotnet sln PinkMachine19.TimeClock.sln list.

concept.title: Three templates, three jobs
paragraphs: dotnet new console generates a project whose .csproj sets <OutputType>Exe</OutputType> and whose starter file has a Main entry point — something the operating system can launch directly. This is what PinkMachine19.TimeClock.App is: a runnable program.

dotnet new classlib generates a project with no OutputType override and no entry point. It compiles to a .dll that only means something once another project references it. This is what PinkMachine19.TimeClock.Domain is: a library of types (Employee, ClockEntry, PayrollService) meant to be consumed, not run on its own.

dotnet new xunit generates a class library too, but one pre-wired with the xUnit and Microsoft.NET.Test.Sdk package references and an <IsPackable>false</IsPackable> setting. Structurally it's a class library; its distinguishing feature is what it's for, not anything the compiler treats differently.
concept.code:
dotnet new classlib -o src/PinkMachine19.TimeClock.Domain
dotnet new console -o src/PinkMachine19.TimeClock.App
dotnet new xunit -o tests/PinkMachine19.TimeClock.Domain.Tests

concept.title: src/ and tests/ are convention, not a compiler rule
paragraphs: Nothing in the .NET toolchain requires a src/ or tests/ folder. PinkMachine19.TimeClock.sln groups its projects under a src solution folder and a tests solution folder purely so dotnet sln list and any IDE's solution explorer show the same two-way split a human would draw by hand: things that ship, and things that check the things that ship.

Creating the solution and adding projects to it are two separate, ordinary CLI steps — dotnet new sln makes the manifest, dotnet sln add registers each project inside it. Neither step writes or moves any source code.
concept.code:
dotnet new sln -n PinkMachine19.TimeClock -f sln
dotnet sln PinkMachine19.TimeClock.sln add src/PinkMachine19.TimeClock.Domain/PinkMachine19.TimeClock.Domain.csproj
dotnet sln PinkMachine19.TimeClock.sln add src/PinkMachine19.TimeClock.App/PinkMachine19.TimeClock.App.csproj
dotnet sln PinkMachine19.TimeClock.sln add tests/PinkMachine19.TimeClock.Domain.Tests/PinkMachine19.TimeClock.Domain.Tests.csproj
dotnet build PinkMachine19.TimeClock.sln

concept.title: Professional layout: a standard folder per purpose
paragraphs: A freshly generated project is one flat folder. As it grows, most .NET codebases converge on the same small set of purpose-named subfolders, because giving each kind of thing its own folder makes the codebase navigable by a stranger without reading every file first. PinkMachine19.TimeClock.Domain (business types and logic), PinkMachine19.TimeClock.Infrastructure (data access), and PinkMachine19.TimeClock.Web (the future HTTP-facing project) each end up needing a different subset of these, based on what that project's job actually is.

Here is the standard set and why each one exists. Configuration/ holds strongly-typed classes that mirror sections of appsettings.json, so configuration is read once into a typed object instead of looked up by raw string key everywhere it's needed. Constants/ holds fixed values — thresholds, format strings, default limits — named once so they aren't duplicated as magic numbers scattered through the code. Dtos/ holds Data Transfer Objects: shapes that cross the HTTP boundary, decoupled from the internal shape of the domain models so either can change independently. Exceptions/ holds domain-specific exception types (an already-clocked-in employee, an invalid payroll period) so callers can catch a precise failure instead of a generic Exception. Extensions/ holds extension methods that add behavior to types the project doesn't own, without subclassing or wrapping them. Helpers/ holds small, stateless utility logic used by more than one class that doesn't naturally belong on any single domain type. Interfaces/ holds contracts like IClockEntryRepository that describe what a collaborator must do, not how, so consumers can depend on behavior instead of a concrete class. Mappings/ holds the translation logic between domain models and Dtos/Requests/Responses, kept in one place so the mapping rules aren't duplicated across every endpoint. Models/ holds the core domain entities — Employee, ClockEntry, Timesheet — independent of any storage format or wire format. Options/ holds classes bound through the Options pattern (IOptions<T>) for configuration that gets injected into services, rather than read as raw values. Repositories/ holds concrete data-access implementations of the interfaces declared in Interfaces/, kept separate so the domain layer never depends on a specific storage technology. Requests/ holds the shapes of incoming API payloads, named for the action they represent (ClockInRequest) so an endpoint's expected input is obvious from the type alone. Responses/ holds the shapes of outgoing API payloads, kept separate from Requests and from domain Models so a response can be shaped for its caller without changing what's stored internally. Services/ holds application logic that coordinates models and repositories to carry out a use case — recording a clock entry, computing payroll. Validators/ holds input-validation logic kept separate from the Dtos it validates, so validation rules can change without touching the shape of the data.

Not every project needs every folder. PinkMachine19.TimeClock.Domain (business rules and data shapes) is where Constants, Exceptions, Extensions, Helpers, Interfaces, Models, and Services belong. PinkMachine19.TimeClock.Infrastructure (data access) is where Repositories belongs, next to the concrete EF Core code it will eventually contain. PinkMachine19.TimeClock.Web (the future HTTP API) is where Configuration, Dtos, Mappings, Options, Requests, Responses, and Validators belong, since those all exist to shape and validate what crosses the wire. The point of this lesson is understanding why each folder exists and where its contents conceptually belong — not memorizing this exact list. A different team might name Helpers/ differently or skip Mappings/ until they actually need it, and that's fine; what matters is that the choice is deliberate.

concept.title: Git tracks files, not folders — so every folder gets a README
paragraphs: Git's index stores blobs (file contents) and trees (directory listings that point at blobs), never a directory entry with nothing inside it. An empty Validators/ folder can sit on your disk for weeks, but the moment you git add . and commit, nothing gets recorded for it — there's no file to point at. Clone the repository fresh, or check out that commit somewhere else, and Validators/ simply isn't there.

The fix is the smallest possible tracked file: a README.md with one or two sentences describing the folder's purpose. This isn't a workaround so much as free documentation — a new contributor opening Requests/README.md immediately knows what belongs there, instead of guessing from an empty directory or waiting for the first file to set the precedent.
concept.code:
mkdir -p src/PinkMachine19.TimeClock.Domain/{Constants,Exceptions,Extensions,Helpers,Interfaces,Models,Services}
mkdir -p src/PinkMachine19.TimeClock.Infrastructure/Repositories
mkdir -p src/PinkMachine19.TimeClock.Web/{Configuration,Dtos,Mappings,Options,Requests,Responses,Validators}

printf '# Models\n\nThe core domain entities, independent of any storage or wire format.\n' > src/PinkMachine19.TimeClock.Domain/Models/README.md

for d in Constants Exceptions Extensions Helpers Interfaces Models Services; do
  test -s "src/PinkMachine19.TimeClock.Domain/$d/README.md" || printf '# %s\n' "$d" > "src/PinkMachine19.TimeClock.Domain/$d/README.md"
done

lab.objective: Reproduce TimeClock's project layout from scratch with the dotnet CLI, then scaffold the standard purpose-named folders and READMEs the real projects will grow into.
lab.startingCondition: The repository already contains a working PinkMachine19.TimeClock.sln with PinkMachine19.TimeClock.Domain, PinkMachine19.TimeClock.App, PinkMachine19.TimeClock.Infrastructure, PinkMachine19.TimeClock.Web, and PinkMachine19.TimeClock.Domain.Tests. You will rebuild the App/Domain/Tests portion from nothing in a separate scratch folder, then create the standard folders directly inside the real repository (folders and READMEs only — no C# code).
steps: In a new empty scratch folder outside this repository, run: dotnet new sln -n PinkMachine19.TimeClock -f sln (the -f sln flag matters: on current SDKs, dotnet new sln defaults to the newer .slnx format, but this repository's solution file is the classic .sln format)
Run: dotnet new classlib -o src/PinkMachine19.TimeClock.Domain, then dotnet new console -o src/PinkMachine19.TimeClock.App, then dotnet new xunit -o tests/PinkMachine19.TimeClock.Domain.Tests

Add all three to the solution with dotnet sln PinkMachine19.TimeClock.sln add for each .csproj path, then run dotnet build PinkMachine19.TimeClock.sln and confirm all three projects build with zero errors

From the real repository root, run dotnet sln PinkMachine19.TimeClock.sln list and compare its project list against what you just built — App/Domain/Tests should match at the same relative paths and depth

Back in the real repository, create the standard folders: mkdir -p src/PinkMachine19.TimeClock.Domain/{Constants,Exceptions,Extensions,Helpers,Interfaces,Models,Services}, mkdir -p src/PinkMachine19.TimeClock.Infrastructure/Repositories, and mkdir -p src/PinkMachine19.TimeClock.Web/{Configuration,Dtos,Mappings,Options,Requests,Responses,Validators}

Write a one- or two-sentence README.md into every folder you just created, explaining that folder's purpose in your own words (not copy-pasted) — for example: printf '# Validators

Input-validation logic kept separate from the Dtos it validates.
' > src/PinkMachine19.TimeClock.Web/Validators/README.md

Run dotnet build PinkMachine19.TimeClock.sln -c Release and dotnet test PinkMachine19.TimeClock.sln -c Release --no-build from the real repository root and confirm both still succeed with zero errors and zero failing tests — the new folders should have no effect on the build at all
lab.expectedBehavior: Your scratch solution builds three projects with zero errors, matching the real repository's App/Domain/Tests paths. All 15 standard folders exist under the correct real project, each containing a non-empty README.md. dotnet build PinkMachine19.TimeClock.sln -c Release and dotnet test PinkMachine19.TimeClock.sln -c Release --no-build both succeed exactly as they did before the folders were added.
lab.validation: dotnet build PinkMachine19.TimeClock.sln -c Release && dotnet test PinkMachine19.TimeClock.sln -c Release --no-build

postQuiz.prompt: You run dotnet new console -o src/PinkMachine19.TimeClock.App but never run dotnet sln add. Later, dotnet build PinkMachine19.TimeClock.sln succeeds with no mention of PinkMachine19.TimeClock.App. Why?
options: Console apps build automatically once created
PinkMachine19.TimeClock.App was never added to the solution, so the solution build has no reason to know it exists
dotnet build always finds every .csproj under the current directory
postQuiz.explanation: A folder on disk and a solution member are two different things. Only dotnet sln add creates the membership dotnet build PinkMachine19.TimeClock.sln relies on.

postQuiz.prompt: You create mkdir -p src/PinkMachine19.TimeClock.Web/Validators, write no files into it, and commit. A teammate clones the repository fresh. What do they see?
options: An empty Validators/ folder, exactly as you left it
No Validators/ folder at all, because git never recorded an empty directory
A build error, because the folder is referenced somewhere
postQuiz.explanation: Git's index only tracks files (and the directory structure implied by their paths). A directory with nothing tracked inside it is invisible to git add and disappears on clone.

postQuiz.prompt: Why does Repositories/ belong under PinkMachine19.TimeClock.Infrastructure rather than PinkMachine19.TimeClock.Domain, even though the repository interfaces (Interfaces/) live in Domain?
options: Infrastructure is just an arbitrary place to put extra folders
Domain should not depend on any specific storage technology, so the concrete, storage-aware implementations live in the project that's allowed to know about EF Core
Interfaces and their implementations must always be in different solutions
postQuiz.explanation: Keeping concrete repository implementations out of Domain is what lets Domain stay reusable by any consumer, regardless of what storage technology that consumer eventually chooses.

reflections: Which command created files on disk, and which command changed what dotnet build PinkMachine19.TimeClock.sln considers in scope?
For one folder you created, could you explain its purpose to someone who has never seen this codebase, without reading the README you wrote?
Why does a README.md count as a legitimate fix for git's empty-directory problem instead of a hack?
whatBreaks: Skipping dotnet sln add leaves a project that builds standalone but is invisible to solution-wide build/test/restore commands. Creating a folder without any tracked file inside it looks fine locally but silently vanishes for every teammate who clones the repository, so any convention that depends on the folder existing (an CI step that globs Validators/*.cs, for instance) breaks for them with no obvious cause. Putting Repositories/ (or any storage-aware code) inside PinkMachine19.TimeClock.Domain instead of PinkMachine19.TimeClock.Infrastructure would make Domain depend on a specific storage technology, undermining the reusability the next session builds on.
summary: A solution is a manifest naming which projects build and test together; a project is the actual buildable unit, created with dotnet new console, classlib, or xunit depending on its job. Beyond that, a mature project organizes its own contents into purpose-named folders — Models, Interfaces, Services, Dtos, Validators, and the rest — chosen deliberately for what that project is responsible for, and every one of those folders needs a tracked file, usually a README.md, or git will not carry it to the next clone.
